description: Who Added Me? is an international team taking on Be An Earth System Trend Detective! We bring together skills in economics, statistics, remote sensing, AI/ML, data engineering, software development, and UX/UI design. We’re exploring NASA Earth data and deciding which variable and region to study. We aim to build an interactive tool that explains what is changing, where, and how significantly. We welcome feedback from people with climate science, time-series, or geospatial expertise.
summary:
Alaska Trend Detective is an interactive, browser-based experience that helps people investigate how Earth-system trends are identified, how they vary by season and time window, and why evidence and uncertainty matter. Its central question is whether near-surface air temperature changed significantly in Interior Alaska from 1980 to 2025.

Using 552 monthly NASA MERRA-2 2-meter air-temperature values, our analysis finds a statistically significant long-term warming trend of about 0.41 °C per decade. We also flag a roughly 0.35 °C step in the record around 1992; excluding that shift gives a lower estimate of about 0.3 °C per decade. Five of 32 tested 15-year windows show cooling, illustrating how a short or selectively chosen period can tell a different story.

The site turns these findings into an interactive Trend Detective experience: visitors can explore seasons and time windows, change analysis settings in the lab, and try short missions that reveal how window choice affects interpretation. The 2015 wildfire season adds environmental context, while fire observations are treated as context rather than proof that fires caused the long-term temperature trend. MERRA-2 is a reanalysis product, and the findings describe the selected study area and period.
details:
Interior Alaska: Be an Earth System Trend Detective is an interactive browser-based research and learning experience built around a specific scientific question: How has near-surface air temperature changed in Interior Alaska from 1980 to 2025, and how do vegetation and fire observations guide permafrost-risk research?

The project brings together three evidence streams: NASA MERRA-2 air temperature, NASA MODIS vegetation observations, and wildfire evidence from NASA burned-area data and fire-perimeter records. Instead of presenting a single trend number without context, the website lets users inspect when and where the signal appears, compare seasons and time windows, examine fire and vegetation layers, and see the methods and limitations alongside the findings.

The study area and datasets

We selected a consistent study box spanning 63–67°N and 155–145°W. The box is a project-defined analysis area, not an official administrative or ecological boundary. We matched the temperature, vegetation and fire context to this same window wherever the available products allowed.

The main climate record is 552 monthly values of NASA MERRA-2 2-meter air temperature from January 1980 through December 2025. MERRA-2 is an atmospheric reanalysis: it combines a modelling system with assimilated observations. We therefore describe it as a reanalysis product, not as a direct satellite-only temperature measurement or a thermometer reading at every point in the study box. NASA documents MERRA-2 as a long-term monthly meteorological dataset that includes 2-meter air temperature.

The vegetation record uses NASA MODIS/Terra MOD13A3.061 monthly EVI at 1 km, with supplied files from March 2000 to December 2025. EVI is a measure of vegetation greenness. It does not identify species, count animals or plants, measure habitat quality, or provide a direct measurement of albedo. We applied the product quality information to distinguish usable observations from quality gaps.

The fire analysis combines NASA MCD64A1.061 burned-area data with fire-perimeter context. Our supplied fire archive has QA and burn-date layers for 2001–2015; the 2015 monthly timing analysis is the main fire result shown in this submission. The map’s 132 perimeter outlines are boundaries, not 132 confirmed unique fires and not burned-area pixels. We keep statewide fire statistics separate from results inside our study box.

What the temperature analysis found

For the complete 1980–2025 record, our approved analysis estimates a warming trend of about +0.41 °C per decade. The AR(1)-adjusted OLS result has a 95% confidence interval of +0.19 to +0.62 °C per decade, with p = 0.00039 and an effective sample size of 45.1 out of 46 annual values. Robustness checks give a Sen slope of about +0.42 °C per decadeand a Mann–Kendall p = 0.00086.

The seasonal analysis shows a particularly clear autumn signal: approximately +0.77 °C per decade for September–November, with a 95% confidence interval of +0.44 to +1.10 °C per decade.

We also checked how the apparent trend changes with the selected period. In our window analysis, the full-period trend first reaches statistical significance with a 35-year record, from 1980 to 2014. Five of the 32 tested 15-year windows show cooling, while every tested 30-year window shows warming. The contrast is one of the project’s central lessons: a short period can tell a different story from a longer record, so users should inspect the window behind a trend claim.

A source-record discontinuity around 1992 requires special care. We identified an approximately 0.35 °C step near a MERRA-2 production-stream change. In a sensitivity analysis that accounts for this step, the estimated warming rate is about +0.31 °C per decade, with a 95% confidence interval of +0.10 to +0.52 °C per decade. We show this sensitivity openly so that the result is not reduced to a headline number.

The 2015 wildfire season: context, not a causal claim

We used the 2015 wildfire season to explore how climate and land observations can be examined together. In the matched study box, our QA-screened monthly burn-date analysis found that 91.3% of counted burned cells occurred in June and July. The count is based on the supplied regridded files and is reported as cell timing and share, not as a verified native-resolution burned-area total.

The temperature record gives important context: the study-box 2015 annual anomaly was +1.01 °C relative to the 1991–2020 baseline; May had the largest monthly positive anomaly at +3.80 °C, while the June–August mean anomaly was −0.45 °C. The main concentration of burn-date cells came after May. This timing comparison raises questions for further research; it does not show that May warmth caused the fires. Daily fire weather, snowmelt, fuels, precipitation, lightning and human ignitions would require separate analysis.

We also place the study in the context of the 2015 statewide fire season, while clearly labelling statewide figures as statewide rather than assigning them to our study box. A contemporary Tanana report documents smoke and disruption to local operations, giving the fire research a human context without treating the regional temperature trend as a fire forecast.

Vegetation, snow, albedo and permafrost

The supplied MODIS EVI record supports 26 complete June–August seasonal summaries. Of 310 monthly raster records, 215 monthly observations pass the project’s strict rank-0 quality screen and 95 are retained as explicit quality gaps rather than silently interpolated. The website reports an approximately 10–13% preliminary change in summer greenness over the available period and a 2015 summer EVI snapshot of 0.359, with 73.4% QA-valid area coverage.

We label the EVI change preliminary and keep its meaning narrow: it is a greenness signal, not a result about species, biodiversity, habitat condition or albedo. We use published research to explain why vegetation, snow cover, fire and albedo matter to permafrost research, while distinguishing that external evidence from measurements made by our team. For example, published work in central Alaska has studied post-fire changes in vegetation, snow dynamics, albedo and radiative forcing; a separate USGS-indexed study modelled wildfire-related active-layer thickening at a specific Alaska site. Neither study is presented as a measurement from our study box.

This distinction matters because the project’s current measured outputs are air temperature, EVI and fire context. They do not directly measure local surface albedo, active-layer thickness, permafrost temperature, species abundance or habitat condition. Those are important next steps for a stronger permafrost-risk assessment.

The interactive experience

The website is designed as both a study dashboard and a detective game:

  • Interactive study dashboard: users can look up the 552 monthly temperature values by month and year, toggle the trend line, view seasonal results and test time windows of ten years or more. The results panel reports the slope, 95% range and p-value for the selected precomputed analysis.
  • Map exploration: users can switch between study and regional framing and between terrain and plain basemaps. The grid view reports that 770 of 819 cells remain significant under the project’s all-cell testing.
  • Vegetation and fire views: visitors can compare 2015 and 2025 summer EVI maps, inspect pixels and the 132 fire-perimeter outlines, and download QA tables, yearly tables and fire GeoJSON.
  • Detective Game: three clues invite players to predict the trend, the minimum detection length and the fastest-warming season before seeing the evidence.
  • Trend Hunt: players select a season and year window, inspect the slope, confidence range and p-value, and view a start-to-end heatmap. Six missions demonstrate how short- and long-window results can differ.
  • Guided Case: an eight-step case asks users to lock in a guess, reveal evidence, test a shorter span, choose a verdict and receive a scored evidence card. Progress saves in the browser.
  • Five-stop tour: a guided introduction leads through the study area, temperature, seasons, fire and land, and sources.
  • Research hub: a separate section connects the evidence to fire, permafrost, albedo, ecosystems and methods using published context.
  • Evidence and interpretation view: visitors can filter 15 findings: nine verified project findings, two preliminary findings and four published findings. The site keeps methods and limitations visible so that a visitor can distinguish our results from preliminary interpretations and external research.

The game is educational and evidence-led. It does not calculate new statistics in the browser, forecast fires, or claim that temperature caused a specific fire or landslide. Its purpose is to help users ask better questions of the data and understand how analytical choices affect interpretation.

Why the project matters

Interior Alaska is a useful pilot area for exploring boreal and permafrost monitoring. A long-term regional temperature signal can help frame questions about frozen ground, vegetation, infrastructure and seasonal change. The project connects those questions to examples such as Denali’s Pretty Rocks landslide and road-replacement work, while making clear that the website does not attribute that local event to our regional trend. The National Park Service describes thawing permafrost as part of the Pretty Rocks context and reports the bridge project’s cost at approximately US$230 million.

The intended users include students and educators learning to interpret Earth-observation data; communities and infrastructure stakeholders using regional trends to frame monitoring questions; and researchers or land stewards looking for areas where additional field checks may be useful. The project is an exploratory research and learning tool, not an operational warning service, route-safety alert or decision system.

What makes the project distinctive

The creative element is the combination of a real, multi-decade NASA data analysis with a playable investigation. Users do not just read “warming detected”; they can make a prediction, choose a season and time window, see how the result changes, inspect the map, and compare that result with vegetation and wildfire context. The interface is built to make uncertainty and evidence part of the experience rather than footnotes hidden after the conclusion.

Tools and development

We built a browser-based web application with a Next.js frontend and a Python FastAPI backend. Python scripts convert and validate NASA Giovanni downloads, process the study data and prepare verified trend results. The project uses CSV time series, GeoJSON fire perimeters and raster-based satellite products. GitHub provides version control and the team’s development workflow; Vercel hosts the API, with the frontend prepared for public deployment.

Limitations and future research

Our study box is a selected analysis area, not an official region, and MERRA-2 is a gridded reanalysis whose regional mean cannot represent every local condition. The 1992 discontinuity affects the estimated rate and is therefore reported with a sensitivity result. Seasonal and rolling-window comparisons are exploratory; statistical significance should not be interpreted as causation.

The vegetation record begins in March 2000, includes explicit quality gaps, and measures greenness rather than species or habitat. The fire perimeter outlines are not burned-area pixels, and our supplied MCD64A1 archive does not support a complete multi-year burned-area total for the full study period. The 2015 fire result is a single-season analysis, not evidence of a long-term fire trend.

Future work could calculate QA-screened burned area on the product’s native grid for all available years; extend fire–temperature–vegetation comparisons across matched periods; add direct albedo and snow-timing observations; compare burned and control sites; and validate satellite-derived findings against field measurements of ground temperature and active-layer thickness. These steps would test the mechanisms more directly without overstating what the current prototype has established.

Team contributions

Alisa Glukhovtsova - team lead, NASA data discovery and research coordination. Led team coordination and presentation preparation. Identified, sourced, retrieved and organized the NASA datasets and supporting research materials used in the project, and helped connect the temperature, vegetation and wildfire evidence to the project’s research question and impact.

Koni - study framing and scientific interpretation. Identified Interior Alaska as a strong pilot area for boreal and permafrost monitoring, developed a path for comparison with similar regions, strengthened the wildfire context, and interpreted temperature and vegetation results into meaningful scientific insights.

Fattah - backend, data pipeline and release workflow. Created the repository and branch workflow, including protection on main; built and deployed the FastAPI backend; developed NASA Giovanni conversion and validation; integrated candidate-region NASA data; documented the API contract and frontend handoff; released approved findings and evidence; and prepared deployment guidance.

Hendraa - interface refinement and user experience, UI/UX. Improved the site’s design, map exploration, temperature-result presentation and mobile layout; connected research data to the frontend; and organized the sources, methods and limitations into a clearer learning flow.

Jennie - Detective Game and data visualization. Designed the Detective Game, including its investigative structure and learning flow. Also modelled the graph comparing Interior Alaska’s annual temperature and summer greenness, scaling each series against its own 2000–2025 average.

Arina - contribution to confirm before submission. Suggested ownership: consolidate and check the sources, evidence and limitation labels across the website and submission.

This project took repeated checking and revision: we aligned the study window across datasets, tested alternative explanations, distinguished a fire perimeter from burned pixels, preserved quality gaps in the vegetation record, and documented a discontinuity in the temperature series. That work shaped both the research and the product. Our goal is not simply to display a warming number, but to let people investigate how it was obtained, what changes when they choose another season or period, and what further evidence is needed to understand the impacts.
